summary:
Colorado stands within the United States federal framework, which sets the baseline a trans visitor carries into the state: Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, the State Department no longer issues the X marker and processes new passports only as M or F, the Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and TSA screening procedures can require secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that disclose a traveller's trans status. Visa discretion over transgender athletes applying to compete in women's sports, flagged with an internal marking and treated in some cases as grounds for a permanent ban, applies at any port of entry including Denver.

State law in Colorado runs against that current. The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act expressly covers gender identity and gender expression across employment, housing and public accommodations, and the legislature expanded that coverage again in 2025. Public-accommodation coverage is the provision a visitor would rely on directly, in hotels, restaurants, shops and venues.

The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on 18 May 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law by suspending gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to enjoin the hospital into resuming puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing the same treatment for cisgender children while halting it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity.' Two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.

Care access still narrows on federal funding. Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage of hormone therapy, puberty blockers and related gender-affirming care for transgender youth from 13 October 2026, because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under 18 and under 19 through the CHP+ child programme. The state Medicaid agency says resuming coverage 'will require legislative action.' Patients already taking hormones retain coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected. A visitor needing continuing care should therefore expect the federal constraint to govern here rather than the state's protective posture.

A July 2026 national risk assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people, alongside California, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey, and counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage.

That posture faces a direct political test. Colorado voters decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender children from gendered sports not aligned with biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after elections officials certified signatures on the measures in March 2026. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and, if passed, would write restrictions on transgender minors into state law.

Incarceration risk in Colorado is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care; a court-approved 2024 consent decree in Denver District Court (Raven v. Polis) required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement, and relief has been won through court order rather than a baseline housing rule.
tangentialFactors:
Colorado's trajectory sits inside a national pattern moving the other way. The July 2026 assessment that lists Colorado among nine protective states simultaneously flags Idaho as the latest 'Do Not Travel' state for trans people, bringing such flags to four, and reports that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights nationally. Kansas enacted a law in February 2026 barring marker changes on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, which rights groups describe as a template for other states.

The federal pressure that produced the Colorado Supreme Court case is not confined to one hospital. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as 'chemical and surgical mutilation of children,' the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for patient records in summer 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for such care. Several federal measures of this kind have been blocked or enjoined in court, which is why litigation outcomes in Colorado and elsewhere remain live rather than settled.

Facilities access is a sharper risk outside Colorado. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with some states making trans bathroom use a criminal offence; in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's law. Colorado has no comparable statute.

Foreign governments have treated the whole United States as a documentation risk: in April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the US, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.
localsOnly:
Colorado residents benefit from health-insurance statutes the July 2026 assessment describes as comprehensive, covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related care, and from anti-discrimination coverage in employment and housing that a visitor cannot claim in the same way.

The Medicaid suspension from 13 October 2026 is a resident-facing programme change: about 500 young people under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, current patients keep coverage during a six-month taper, and behavioural healthcare continues. The state agency's statement that restarting coverage requires legislative action indicates the timeline for reversal runs through the Colorado General Assembly.

Placement in state custody is regulated by the 2024 Raven v. Polis consent decree rather than by statute. The decree required the Colorado Department of Corrections to expand health care, to open a 100-bed voluntary specialised unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison, and to pay roughly $2.1 million to about 400 class members. A 2019 settlement over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison, Lindsay Saunders-Velez, paid $170,000.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Colorado voters adopt Initiatives 109 and 110 in November 2026 is unresolved in the sources available here; the measures were certified for the ballot in March 2026 and no outcome is sourced.

The sources do not document whether Children's Hospital Colorado fully complied with the injunction ordered on 18 May 2026, or whether the hospital or the state sought further review of the 5-2 decision.

Whether the August 2026 federal Medicaid rule is under challenge, and whether any stay could restore coverage before 13 October 2026, is not sourced. The state agency's statement about legislative action is the only cited path to resumption.

Enforcement of the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act in hotels, restaurants and retail venues against a misgendering or refusing visitor is not sourced here; the coverage is statutory, but no complaint or penalty data for public accommodations is available in this inventory.

Post-2024 compliance monitoring of the Raven v. Polis consent decree, including the current status of the Sterling and women's-prison units, is not sourced beyond the decree's terms.
